paraphrase: Chapter 7 moves in eight steps. (1) 7.1–3: with his mind attached to the Lord, practising yoga and taking refuge in him, Arjuna will know him entirely (samagram) and without doubt; the Lord will declare knowledge together with vijñāna, after which nothing further remains to be known; among thousands scarcely one strives for perfection, and of those who strive scarcely one knows him in truth. (2) 7.4–7: his two natures — the lower, divided eightfold (earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of 'I'), and the higher, which has become the living being and by which the world is upheld; all beings have these two as their womb; he is the origin and the dissolution of the whole world; nothing is higher than him, and all this is strung on him like gems on a thread. (3) 7.8–12: he is the essence in things — the taste in water, the light of moon and sun, Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, fragrance in earth, brilliance in fire, life in all beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed of beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the strength of the strong free of desire and passion, desire not opposed to dharma; the states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from him, yet he is not in them — they are in him. (4) 7.13–15: deluded by these guṇa-made states the world does not know him; his divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross, but those who take refuge in him alone cross it; evil-doers of demonic disposition, their knowledge carried off by māyā, do not take refuge in him. (5) 7.16–19: four kinds of people of good deeds worship him — the distressed, the one who wishes to know, the seeker of gain and the knower; all are noble, but the knower, ever yoked and of single devotion, is foremost, mutually dear with him and held by him to be his very self; at the end of many births the knower takes refuge in him, knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' — a great soul very hard to find. (6) 7.20–23: those whose knowledge desires have carried off resort to other deities, following their observances; whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, he makes that faith firm, and through it the worshipper obtains desires ordained by him; but the fruit is finite — worshippers of the gods go to the gods, his devotees come to him. (7) 7.24–26: the unintelligent think of him as unmanifest come into manifestation, not knowing his higher, imperishable state; veiled by his yoga-māyā he is not manifest to all; he knows all beings past, present and to come, but no one knows him. (8) 7.27–30: all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs born of desire and aversion; those of meritorious deeds whose sin has ended worship him firm in their vows; those who take refuge in him and strive for release from old age and death know Brahman, the adhyātma and action completely, and those who know him with the adhibhūta, the adhidaiva and the adhiyajña know him even at the time of departure — terms that Arjuna asks about in 8.1–2. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to give the knowledge of the Lord 'entire' (samagra), together with vijñāna, and to show refuge in him as the way across his māyā.

paraphrase: Chapter 8 moves in nine steps. (1) 8.1–2: Arjuna asks seven questions — what is that Brahman, what is the adhyātma, what is action, what are the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva, who and how is the adhiyajña here in the body, and how is the Lord to be known at the time of departure by the self-controlled. (2) 8.3–4: the Lord's answers: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; own being (svabhāva) is called the adhyātma; the sending-forth (visarga) that brings about beings' states of existence is called action; the adhibhūta is the perishable state, the adhidaivata puruṣa ('person'), and the adhiyajña the Lord himself, here in the body. (3) 8.5–8: whoever departs at the end remembering him alone comes to his state; one goes to whatever state one remembers on leaving the body, having always been shaped by it; therefore Arjuna is to remember him at all times and fight, with mind and intellect offered to him; with thought (cetas) yoked by the yoga of repeated practice one goes to the supreme divine Person. (4) 8.9–13: the departure of one who remembers: whoever at departure, with unmoving mind, devotion and the power of yoga, the breath made to enter between the brows, remembers the ancient seer, subtler than the subtle, sun-coloured, beyond darkness, reaches that supreme divine Person; the imperishable that knowers of the Veda speak of and ascetics enter is declared in brief: whoever departs having restrained the gates, confined the mind in the heart and placed the breath in the head, uttering Oṃ, the one-syllabled Brahman, and remembering him, goes to the supreme goal. (5) 8.14–16: for the ever-yoked yogin who remembers him constantly with thought on nothing else (ananya-cetas) he is easy to reach; the great souls who come to him are not reborn into the impermanent abode of sorrow, whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return. (6) 8.17–19: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand yugas and his night as long; at the coming of day manifest things come forth from the unmanifest, at the coming of night they dissolve into it, and the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly. (7) 8.20–22: beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest being that does not perish when all beings perish; it is called the imperishable and the supreme goal, from which they do not return — his supreme abode; that supreme Person, in whom beings abide and by whom all is pervaded, is gained by undivided devotion. (8) 8.23–27: the times at which departing yogins go to non-return or to return: fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the six months of the northern course lead the knowers of Brahman to Brahman; smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the six months of the southern course lead the yogin to the lunar light and return; these two courses are everlasting for the world, and knowing them no yogin is deluded — so Arjuna is to be yoked in yoga at all times. (9) 8.28: having known this, the yogin goes beyond all the merit declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts and reaches the supreme, primal place. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the questions left open at 7.29–30, above all how the Lord is known at death, and to show that constant remembrance of him, carried through to the moment of departure, leads to the imperishable from which there is no return.

paraphrase: Chapter 9 moves in nine steps. (1) 9.1–3: to Arjuna, who does not cavil, the Lord will declare the most secret knowledge together with vijñāna, knowing which he will be freed from what is inauspicious — the royal knowledge, the royal secret, the supreme purifier, directly apprehended, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise, imperishable; those without faith in this dharma do not reach him and return to the path of death and saṃsāra. (2) 9.4–10: all this is pervaded by him in unmanifest form; all beings abide in him, but he is not established in them — and yet beings do not abide in him: 'behold my lordly yoga'; his self sustains beings and brings them into being without abiding in them, as the great wind always abides in space; at the close of a kalpa beings go into his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth again, taking hold of his own prakṛti; these acts do not bind him, seated as one indifferent and unattached; with him as overseer prakṛti gives birth to the moving and the unmoving, and so the world revolves. (3) 9.11–12: the deluded disregard him who has taken on a human body, not knowing his higher state as the great Lord of beings; of vain hopes, vain acts and vain knowledge, they resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras. (4) 9.13–15: the great souls, resorting to the divine nature, worship him with minds on nothing else — always glorifying him, striving, firm in their vows, bowing to him with devotion, ever yoked — and others worship him by the sacrifice of knowledge, as one, as distinct and in many ways.
